Census Data of Maryland Counties

Savannah Normand

2026-10-09

  • Tidying up the data :)
  • Optional: My viewing and exporting of the tidy data set
  • Graph 1: Population change from 2020 to 2025

  • Graph 3: Racial and ethnic composition in 2025
  • Reflection Time

These graphs compare population trends, average population, and racial and ethnic composition across Maryland’s 23 counties and Baltimore city. Population estimates refer to July 1. Baltimore city is a county equivalent, separate from Baltimore County.

Tidying up the data :)

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, dpi = 160, out.width = "100%")

county_pop <- read.csv(
  "https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/counties/totals/co-est2025-alldata.csv",
  fileEncoding = "latin1"
)

county_pop <- county_pop |>
  mutate(
    GEOID = sprintf("%02d%03d", STATE, COUNTY),
    NAME = paste0(CTYNAME, ", ", STNAME)
  ) |>
  select(
    STATE,
    COUNTY,
    GEOID,
    NAME,
    starts_with("POPESTIMATE"),
    starts_with("NPOPCHG")
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^(POPESTIMATE|NPOPCHG)[0-9]{4}$"),
    names_to = c(".value", "year"),
    names_pattern = "(POPESTIMATE|NPOPCHG)([0-9]{4})"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year)
  ) |>
  filter(year %in% 2020:2025)

county_demo <- read.csv(
  "https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/counties/asrh/cc-est2025-alldata.csv",
  fileEncoding = "latin1"
)

county_demo <- county_demo |>
  mutate(
    year = case_when(
      YEAR == 2 ~ 2020,
      YEAR == 3 ~ 2021,
      YEAR == 4 ~ 2022,
      YEAR == 5 ~ 2023,
      YEAR == 6 ~ 2024,
      YEAR == 7 ~ 2025
    ),
    GEOID = sprintf("%02d%03d", STATE, COUNTY),
    NAME = paste0(CTYNAME, ", ", STNAME)
  ) |>
  filter(year %in% 2020:2025)

county_all <- county_demo |>
  left_join(
    county_pop |>
      select(GEOID, NAME, year, POPESTIMATE, NPOPCHG),
    by = c("GEOID", "NAME", "year")
  )

county_all <- county_all |>
  select(
    GEOID,
    NAME,
    year,
    AGEGRP,
    POPESTIMATE,
    NPOPCHG,
    everything()
  )

county_all <- county_all |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.character),
      ~ iconv(.x, from = "latin1", to = "UTF-8", sub = "")
    )
  )

county_all <- county_all |>
  arrange(GEOID, year, AGEGRP)

maryland <- county_all |>
  filter(STATE == 24, COUNTY != 0, AGEGRP == 0) |>
  mutate(county = sub(", Maryland$", "", NAME))

Optional: My viewing and exporting of the tidy data set

View(county_all)

write.csv(
  county_all,
  "C:/Users/savno/Downloads/county_population_demographics_2020_2025.csv",
  row.names = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

Graph 1: Population change from 2020 to 2025

Five panels group counties by their 2020 population size. Every panel uses the same percentage-change scale, making changes from 2020 to 2025 easier to compare. Direct labels identify counties and their total percentage change.

chart_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 19),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 13),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(15, 20, 15, 15)
  )

county_levels <- sort(unique(maryland$county))
county_colors <- setNames(scales::hue_pal()(length(county_levels)), county_levels)

stopifnot(nrow(maryland) == 24 * 6,
          !anyDuplicated(maryland[c("GEOID", "year")]),
          all(is.finite(maryland$POPESTIMATE)),
          all(maryland$POPESTIMATE > 0))
trend_data <- maryland |>
  group_by(GEOID, county) |>
  mutate(percent_change = 100 * (POPESTIMATE / POPESTIMATE[year == 2020] - 1)) |>
  ungroup()

panel_groups <- trend_data |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  arrange(POPESTIMATE) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(ntile(POPESTIMATE, 5), levels = 1:5,
                        labels = c("Smallest counties", "Smaller counties",
                                   "Mid-sized counties", "Larger counties",
                                   "Largest counties"))) |>
  select(GEOID, panel)

trend_data <- trend_data |>
  left_join(panel_groups, by = "GEOID")

end_labels <- trend_data |>
  filter(year == 2025) |>
  mutate(label = paste0(sub(" County$", "", county), "  ",
                        sprintf("%+.1f%%", percent_change)))

graph1 <- ggplot(trend_data,
                 aes(year, percent_change, group = county, color = county)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = end_labels, aes(label = label),
    nudge_x = 0.35, direction = "y", hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
    box.padding = 0.35, min.segment.length = 0,
    segment.alpha = 0.6, max.overlaps = Inf, seed = 24
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = county_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2020:2025, limits = c(2020, 2027.3),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title = "Population trends in Maryland counties, 2020–2025",
       subtitle = "Five groups by 2020 population size; percentage change relative to 2020",
       x = "Year", y = "Population change since 2020 (%)") +
  chart_theme + theme(legend.position = "none",
                      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13))

print(graph1)

Graph 2: Average county population

Each bar shows the mean of the six July population estimates, with a number label rounded to the nearest resident. Colors identify geographic groups used for this chart (listed explicitly in the code). A zero-based linear scale preserves meaningful bar lengths. A log-scale dot plot is available in the optional code below if proportional differences are the focus.

average_data <- maryland |>
  group_by(GEOID, county) |>
  summarise(average_population = mean(POPESTIMATE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    region = case_when(
      county %in% c("Allegany County", "Garrett County", "Washington County") ~ "Western",
      county %in% c("Frederick County", "Montgomery County", "Prince George's County") ~ "Capital",
      county %in% c("Calvert County", "Charles County", "St. Mary's County") ~ "Southern",
      county %in% c("Caroline County", "Cecil County", "Dorchester County", "Kent County",
                    "Queen Anne's County", "Somerset County", "Talbot County",
                    "Wicomico County", "Worcester County") ~ "Eastern Shore",
      TRUE ~ "Central"
    ),
    county = reorder(county, average_population)
  )
region_colors <- c("Western" = "#9366CB", "Capital" = "#387FC8",
                   "Southern" = "#DF8649", "Eastern Shore" = "#279F91", "Central" = "#D4679A")

graph2 <- ggplot(average_data, aes(average_population, county, fill = region)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(round(average_population))),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub(" County$", "", x)) +
  labs(title = "Average population of Maryland counties, 2020–2025",
       subtitle = "Mean of six annual population estimates; labels rounded to the nearest resident",
       x = "Average population", y = NULL, fill = "Geographic group") +
  chart_theme + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

print(graph2)

ggplot(average_data, aes(average_population, county, color = region)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(round(average_population))), hjust = -0.2, size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = region_colors) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.25))) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub(" County$", "", x)) +
  labs(title = "Average county population on a log scale",
       x = "Average population (log scale)", y = NULL, color = "Geographic group") +
  chart_theme + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Graph 3: Racial and ethnic composition in 2025

Each bar adds to 100%. The same seven mutually exclusive groups appear in the same order in every county. Hispanic residents of any race form one group; the other six groups contain non-Hispanic residents only. White, Black, Asian, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander categories refer to race alone. Counties are ordered by their non-Hispanic White share. A majority means more than 50%, whereas the largest group may be less than 50%.

group_order <- c("White", "Black", "Hispanic", "Asian", "Multiracial", "AIAN", "NHPI")
group_colors <- c("White" = "#7798CF", "Black" = "#E49B56", "Hispanic" = "#38AF98",
                  "Asian" = "#B588D5", "Multiracial" = "#E4BF60", "AIAN" = "#D17B88", "NHPI" = "#808A96")

demo_wide <- maryland |>
  filter(year == 2025) |>
  transmute(county, TOT_POP,
            White = NHWA_MALE + NHWA_FEMALE,
            Black = NHBA_MALE + NHBA_FEMALE,
            Hispanic = H_MALE + H_FEMALE,
            Asian = NHAA_MALE + NHAA_FEMALE,
            Multiracial = NHTOM_MALE + NHTOM_FEMALE,
            AIAN = NHIA_MALE + NHIA_FEMALE,
            NHPI = NHNA_MALE + NHNA_FEMALE)
stopifnot(all(rowSums(as.data.frame(demo_wide[group_order])) == demo_wide$TOT_POP))

county_order <- demo_wide |>
  arrange(White / TOT_POP) |>
  pull(county)

demo_long <- demo_wide |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(group_order), names_to = "group", values_to = "population") |>
  mutate(share = population / TOT_POP,
         group = factor(group, levels = group_order),
         county = factor(county, levels = county_order),
         label = ifelse(share >= 0.02, scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1), ""))

graph3 <- ggplot(demo_long, aes(share, county, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.78, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE),
            size = 3.6, color = "#111111") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colors, breaks = group_order) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub(" County$", "", x)) +
  labs(title = "Racial and ethnic composition of Maryland counties, 2025",
       subtitle = "Ordered by non-Hispanic White share",
       x = "Share of county population", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "All groups except Hispanic are non-Hispanic. Labels shown for shares ≥3%; rounded labels may not total 100%.\nAIAN: American Indian/Alaska Native. NHPI: Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander.") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
  chart_theme + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
                      plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 11))

print(graph3)

Reflection Time

I went through multiple iterations of this draft and by far the one that ended up being changed the most was the first graph. I really liked the idea of using a sloped bar chart, but the more I tried to work with it the more I realized it wasn’t really working for this data. I tried splitting it up into 5 graphs, and still knew it wasn’t showing the changes as much as I wanted. Therefore, I pivoted to make the graph show percent change relative to the first year of data, 2020. I think this graph better captures what I wanted to be able to see within the first graph, the relative change over time. I did want to maintain the knowledge about the size of the county populations, since that was lost when shifting towards the new graph, which is why I ended up grouping them by population size.

The least changed graph was my second one, which was pretty cohesive from my first draft. I made some small edits for detail, including adding in the numbers after the bars and color coding them by geographic region as my classmate Chris suggested. Yet, I find this graph to be most satisfying to me, as it was extremely minimal and straightforward at conveying data. I did maintain this graph as average population because, while I discussed it not being a typical statistic used by researchers, it has great merit when a researcher is looking more for the average size of a county over a longer time period, rather than being concerned with the trends of population change within the county. Knowledge about the average size of a county is useful when looking at longer term policy changes, rather than knowing the year to year population size change.

My third graph ended up being a stacked bar chart thanks to the suggestions of my classmate Daniel, which was greatly appreciated, since it displays all information far better than my original regular bar chart did. I went through multiple versions, ultimately landing on the one I have now that remove a dotted line at the 50% part, which I originally had included. I also made sure to display percentage of the demographic if it was 2% or greater, which was the smallest number that could comfortably be displayed within the graph without the text bleeding over to the next group.

Overall, I found that Maryland as a whole is growing as a state. Most counties experienced a rise in their population between 2020 and 2025. Interestingly, the ones who lost population ended up being both the most rural areas, such as Garrett county, and the most urban ones, mainly Baltimore city. This shows that more and more people are likely flocking to suburban areas than rural or urban areas as a whole.

I also learned that the majority of Marylands’ most populated counties exist near as suburbs of the Capital, Washington D.C. or in the central part of the state near Baltimore city and interstate 95. The Southern parts of the state run in the middle of the pack while the Eastern Shore and Western part of the states make up nearly all of the smallest average populations from 2020-2025.

Finally, I learned that Maryland is still a primarily white state, with the majority of counties having the white population taking up the largest share of the overall population in comparison to other demographic groups. Uniquely, Maryland did have three places where the black population dominated: Charles county, Baltimore city, and Prince George’s county. I was especially surprised by the diversity in Charles county, which exists as an urban/suburban area of Washington, D.C. and still had similar levels of diversity as Baltimore city itself. Prince George’s county again exists as an outlier among peers, with it’s extremely rare status of having traditional minority demographics actually existing as the majority, with non-Hispanic White people only taking up 11% in comparison to non-Hispanic Black people making up 57% and Hispanic people taking up 25%.

This project, and class as a whole, was extremely enjoyable and I am truly grateful for the skills I have gained from this project. Thank you!
